evals.prompt: Write a stack data structure in Python. It should support push, pop, and peek. Pop and peek on an empty stack should raise an error.
evals.expected_output: A Stack class built test-first: a [TEST] list, then one test at a time through red, green, and refactor, with minimal code at each step and a commit at each green
expectations: The mode is announced once at the start (TDD mode: auto unless the user asked for human)
A [TEST] list exists before any test or production code is written
Exactly one test is written at a time; the list is never converted into a batch of tests
Every test has setup, invocation, and an assertion, with blank lines between given, when, and then
Each expected value is stated by reasoning before the run; none is copied from a run's output
A prediction is stated before every test run
When a test names something new, a compile or resolution failure is seen before the assertion failure
Only the simplest change is made to pass each test; hard-coded returns appear early and are generalized by later tests
No refactoring happens while a test is red
A refactoring step is considered after every green and either described or stated as none
A commit is made at every green and after each refactoring, with a message naming the behavior
Any test that passes without ever failing is called out with its cause
Error cases (pop and peek on empty) are tested after the happy paths, and the stack still works after a failed pop
The loop ends only when the list is empty and a closing check for remaining concerns has been made

evals.prompt: I need a function that converts Roman numerals to integers in TypeScript. Handle I through M, including subtractive notation like IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, and CM.
evals.expected_output: A converter grown incrementally through TDD from single numerals to additive sequences to subtractive pairs, with the implementation generalizing only as tests demand
expectations: A [TEST] list is written first and starts with the simplest case (a single numeral)
Subtractive cases appear on the list after the additive ones and are implemented only when their test is red
Each test is seen to fail before the code that passes it is written
Expected integer values are derived by reasoning, not by running the function
The implementation grows one case at a time; no complete lookup-table solution is dropped in to pass the first test
Discovered cases (for example, invalid input) are appended to the list rather than implemented on the spot
Refactoring happens on green, in its own step, and does not introduce an abstraction at the first duplication
Invalid-input handling is deferred until the happy paths pass
All previous tests are run at every green, not only the new one
A commit follows each green and each refactoring

evals.prompt: Build a simple shopping cart in Java. It should add items with a name and price, calculate the total, and apply a percentage discount. Don't worry about persistence.
evals.expected_output: A ShoppingCart developed through the loop: empty cart first, then one item, many items, then discount cases, with domain concepts emerging in refactoring rather than designed up front
expectations: The first test is the simplest forcing case (an empty cart's total is zero or equivalent)
Discount logic is not implemented until a discount test is red
The two-step red is visible whenever a new class or method is introduced: compile error, then assertion failure
After each green the newly added lines are checked against the question of whether a failing test requires them
Any domain concept that is introduced (for example a Money type) appears in a refactoring step with no new behavior and tests still green
No test verifies method calls on a mock; every assertion is on a returned value or resulting state
No expected total is pasted from a test run
Commits are made at each green and each refactoring
The loop ends with an explicit check for behaviors that still cause concern, which are added to the list if any
